title: How to Evaluate Preformed Particle Gels for Conformance Control Using Core-Flooding Tests: A Critical Review of Experimental Methods, Procedures, and Guidelines
content: Preformed particle gels (PPGs) have been widely applied to control preferential flow through high-conductivity reservoir pathways and thereby improve waterflood conformance in mature oilfields. Although numerous core-flooding tests have been conducted to investigate PPG transport, plugging, oil displacement, and flow redistribution, the reliability and interpretation of these published results vary substantially. This paper critically examines experimental procedures and published data from approximately 200 experiments reported across a large number of publications, with particular attention to the distinction between particle entry, propagation, and retention. For injectivity tests, continuously increasing injection pressure or a small volume of injected suspension cannot, by itself, demonstrate successful transport through a core; the pressure response must be interpreted together with particle loading and evidence of penetration. For plugging tests, residual resistance factor must be evaluated under well-defined flow conditions and interpreted considering possible inlet accumulation. Data comparisons show that particle strength, deformability, size relative to pore restrictions, and medium permeability jointly control transport and flow resistance. Displacement experiments require separate accounting of oil produced during particle injection and subsequent waterflooding, whereas parallel-core experiments reveal that not only permeability contrast alone, but also the absolute permeabilities of each core influence the selective diversion. Based on these findings, practical recommendations are developed for test design, reporting, interpretation, and the limits of extrapolating laboratory results to field conformance control.
